chapter_title: Interacting with Smart Contract Data (Read Operations)

screens.title: Interacting with Smart Contract Data
screens.subtitle: Read-only calls with web3.eth.Contract, ABI, and React integration

narration.text: In this chapter you'll learn how a dApp reads data from a deployed smart contract, why that requires the contract's ABI and address, and how to surface that data in React with safe lifecycle handling. We'll start by creating a web3. eth. Contract instance using the ABI and the deployed address. Then we'll call read-only functions — those marked view or pure — using the. call() method which fetches values without sending transactions or spending gas. You'll also see a practical React pattern: using the useEffect hook to fetch contract state when web3, the contract instance, or the connected account changes. The lesson includes a complete example: a SimpleStorage contract that exposes a stored string and a pure number. You'll inspect a custom hook that manages the contract instance, fetches getData and getNumber, handles loading and errors, and exposes a refetch function. Finally we cover common mistakes like calling methods before the contract instance exists, and formatting raw blockchain data for users. By the end you'll know how to wire a contract to state and present contract values in a predictable, testable way.

keyIdea.title: Core idea
keyIdea.text: Read-only contract calls use ABI + address to create a contract instance and .call() to get data without gas; tie calls into React using useEffect to keep UI in sync.

screens.title: Creating a web3.eth.Contract instance
screens.subtitle: Why ABI and address are required and how to instantiate safely

narration.text: A contract instance is the bridge between your dApp and the functions of a deployed smart contract. The instance requires two concrete pieces of information: the contract's ABI, which describes every public function and event, and the contract's deployed address on the current network. Without the ABI, web3 cannot encode calls or decode returns; without the address, it doesn't know where to send the request. Instantiation is a single line in web3: you pass the ABI array and the address to new web3. eth. Contract. A typical pattern keeps the ABI as a JSON import and the address in an environment variable so builds remain portable. A common error is to attempt instantiation before web3 is ready—always check web3 exists and the address is defined. For example, you will often see a try/catch around new web3. eth. Contract to report malformed ABIs or missing addresses. As a concrete example, imagine the SimpleStorage ABI imported from src/contracts/SimpleStorage. json and an address stored in VITE_SIMPLE_STORAGE_CONTRACT_ADDRESS; you create the instance, set it in state, and then use its methods. Misconception to avoid: the contract instance is a local JavaScript object, not an on-chain entity—calls route through your node or provider, and. call() executes a read locally. How will you ensure your web3 and address are present before creating the instance?

keyIdea.title: Instance rule
keyIdea.text: Always supply ABI + address and guard creation with checks for web3 and a valid address to avoid runtime errors.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.4 › Creating a Contract
Core definition
A contract instance is a web3 object created with an ABI and deployed address; it exposes methods that map to the contract's public functions and events.
Code example
// Import ABI (JSON) and read address from env
import SimpleStorageABI from '../contracts/SimpleStorage.json';
const address = import.meta.env.VITE_SIMPLE_STORAGE_CONTRACT_ADDRESS;

// Create contract instance (guard web3 existence)
if (web3 && address) {
  try {
    const simpleStorage = new web3.eth.Contract(SimpleStorageABI, address);
    // use simpleStorage.methods.someFunction()...
  } catch (err) {
    console.error('Failed to create contract instance:', err);
  }
}
Why it matters
Without the ABI you can't call functions; without the address the instance cannot target the deployed contract.
Misconception
The contract object is not on-chain; it's a local API wrapper that encodes calls and sends them to your provider.
Practical checklist
  • Keep ABI in src/contracts and load via import to avoid string errors.
  • Store address in an env variable so it can change per network.
  • Guard instantiation with if (web3 && address) and try/catch to surface ABI/address errors.
  • Log the created instance to confirm methods exist before calling.
Key Takeaway

Instantiate only after web3 is ready and address is present. Treat the ABI as the contract's API spec.

screens.title: ABI and Contract Address
screens.subtitle: What the ABI describes and why the address matters

narration.text: The ABI, or Application Binary Interface, is a JSON description of a contract's public functions, inputs, outputs, and events. It is the contract's A P I in a format web3. js can read. When you import the ABI into your JavaScript code, web3 relies on it to correctly encode function calls and decode the responses sent back by the node. The contract address is the unique location on a particular network where the contract is deployed. Together they let your client know what to call and where to call it. A practical convention is to keep the ABI file inside src/contracts so tooling can import it directly, and to store the deployed address in an environment variable like VITE_SIMPLE_STORAGE_CONTRACT_ADDRESS so you can switch networks without changing source files. A common mistake is to forget to update the address after deploying to a testnet or mainnet; another is to mix up different ABIs from similar contracts. Always confirm the ABI corresponds exactly to the deployed bytecode. Example: if your SimpleStorage JSON doesn't match the deployed contract, methods may be undefined or return decoding errors. How will you confirm ABI and address match before calling methods?

keyIdea.title: ABI + address
keyIdea.text: The ABI defines the contract's callable API; the address points to the deployed instance. Both must match the deployed contract.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.4 › ABI & Address
ABI (Application Binary Interface)
A JSON array describing public functions, their inputs, and outputs so web3 can encode and decode calls.
Example snippet
[
  {
    "inputs": [],
    "name": "getData",
    "outputs": [{ "type": "string" }],
    "stateMutability": "view",
    "type": "function"
  },
  {
    "name": "getNumber",
    "outputs": [{ "type": "uint256" }],
    "stateMutability": "pure",
    "type": "function"
  }
]
Tip
Keep ABI files in src/contracts and import them to avoid manual JSON parsing errors.
Contract Address
A hexadecimal identifier where the contract is deployed on a particular network. Store it in an env var per network.
Env example
VITE_SIMPLE_STORAGE_CONTRACT_ADDRESS=0xYourDeployedContractAddressHere
Common mistake
Using an address from a different network or forgetting to replace a placeholder address causes call failures.

screens.title: Calling view and pure functions with .call()
screens.subtitle: How .call() executes read-only functions and returns values

narration.text: View and pure functions are read-only by definition: view reads on-chain state without changing it, pure uses only input parameters and does not read state. Calling them from web3. js uses the. call() helper which executes the function locally via an Ethereum node and returns a Promise with the result. The process is simple: ensure the contract instance exists, invoke contract. methods. myFunction(... args). call(), await the Promise, and update state with the returned value. Because. call() doesn't create a transaction, it doesn't require a signer or gas; any node can execute it. As a concrete example, calling simpleStorageContract. methods. getData(). call() returns the stored string, and simpleStorageContract. methods. getNumber(). call() returns the pure number 123 in the example contract. A common misconception is thinking. call() will change state—only sending a signed transaction via. send() modifies the chain. Another pitfall: forgetting to await. call() or failing to wrap the call in try/catch, which can leave the UI with stale values or unhandled rejections. Closing thought: when you need a free read,. call() is your tool; when you intend to write, prepare a signed transaction instead.

keyIdea.title: .call() behavior
keyIdea.text: .call() executes read-only functions locally, returns a Promise with the value, and does not require gas or a signer.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.4 › Calling .call()
Step-by-step
  1. Ensure contract instance exists and methods are defined.
  2. Invoke contract.methods.myViewOrPure(...args).call() and await the result.
  3. Handle errors with try/catch and set loading flags while awaiting.
  4. Update component state so the UI renders the returned value.
Concrete example
// Read stored string and a pure number
const name = await simpleStorageContract.methods.getData().call();
const number = await simpleStorageContract.methods.getNumber().call();
Notes & pitfalls
  • .call() does not change state; use .send() for transactions that modify contract storage.
  • Calls execute via the node and will fail if the node or provider is unreachable.
  • Always await and wrap in try/catch to avoid unhandled promise rejections.
  • Large or complex returns (arrays/tuples) may require destructuring or mapping for display.
Key Takeaway

Use .call() for free reads, and guard calls to keep your UI stable and predictable.

screens.title: Using useEffect to fetch contract data
screens.subtitle: When to fetch and how to update component state safely

narration.text: React's useEffect hook is the natural place to run asynchronous reads from a contract because it lets you react to changes in dependencies like your web3 provider, contract instance, account, or network. The typical pattern is to define an async function inside useEffect, check that web3 and the contract instance exist, then call the contract methods with. call() and set component state. Use dependencies to re-run the effect when the provider or contract changes, and memoize the fetch function with useCallback when you plan to expose it. As a concrete example, fetch a contract name on mount: inside useEffect create fetchContractName, check if web3 and contractInstance are ready, await contractInstance. methods. getName(). call(), and call setContractName(name). Wrap it with try/catch to capture network or decoding errors. A common misconception is putting an async function directly into the effect callback; instead define and immediately invoke the async function to avoid returning a Promise from the effect. Finally, keep loading and error flags in state so the UI communicates progress. What dependency list will you choose to ensure timely updates without excessive calls?

keyIdea.title: useEffect pattern
keyIdea.text: Define an async fetch inside useEffect, guard against missing dependencies, handle errors, and include relevant dependencies to re-run the fetch.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.4 › useEffect Integration
Common pattern
Run an async fetch in useEffect, guard web3 and contract, set loading, and update state on success or set error on failure.
useEffect(() => {
  const fetchContractName = async () => {
    if (web3 && contractInstance) {
      try {
        const name = await contractInstance.methods.getName().call();
        setContractName(name);
      } catch (error) {
        console.error('Error fetching contract name:', error);
      }
    }
  };
  fetchContractName();
}, [web3, contractInstance]);
Misconception
Don't return an async function directly from useEffect; define and invoke it inside the effect.
Dependency choices
Include web3, contractInstance, currentAccount, or chainId as dependencies so data refreshes when the environment changes.
Pro tip
Use useCallback for fetch functions if you export them from a hook to avoid unnecessary effect reruns.
Check your understanding
Why include chainId in the dependency list if your app supports multiple networks?

screens.title: Building the useSimpleStorage hook
screens.subtitle: Manage contract instance, fetch data, loading state, error handling, and refetch

narration.text: A custom hook encapsulates contract setup and data fetching so components stay focused on presentation. The useSimpleStorage hook in the example imports the ABI, reads the contract address from import. meta. env, and manages several pieces of state: the contract instance, storedData, contractNumber, a loading flag, and an error message. In the initial effect it creates the contract instance when web3 becomes available, guarding with if (web3 && contractAddress). The fetchContractData function then calls getData and getNumber with. call(), updates state, and sets loading and error flags appropriately. This hook returns the contract, the values, a loading boolean, error text, and a fetchContractData function so callers can re-trigger a refresh on demand. Encapsulating this logic improves code reuse and makes unit testing easier because you can mock the hook. A common pitfall is not memoizing fetchContractData with useCallback when it's a dependency for another effect, which can accidentally cause loops. How would you test this hook to confirm it handles network errors and re-fetch behavior? Building the useSimpleStorage hook means encapsulate instantiation and fetching in a hook that returns data, loading state, error, and a refetch function for consumers.. In practical terms, manage contract instance, fetch data, loading state, error handling, and refetch. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Hook pattern
keyIdea.text: Encapsulate instantiation and fetching in a hook that returns data, loading state, error, and a refetch function for consumers.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.4 › useSimpleStorage Hook
Hook responsibilities
  • Create and store the contract instance when web3 is ready.
  • Expose storedData and contractNumber as stateful values.
  • Provide isLoading and error for UI feedback.
  • Offer fetchContractData as a refetch mechanism.
Example code excerpt
useEffect(() => {
  if (web3 && contractAddress) {
    try {
      const instance = new web3.eth.Contract(SimpleStorageABI, contractAddress);
      setSimpleStorageContract(instance);
    } catch (err) {
      setError('Failed to load contract.');
    }
  }
}, [web3, chainId]);

const fetchContractData = useCallback(async () => {
  if (!simpleStorageContract) return;
  setIsLoadingContractData(true);
  try {
    const data = await simpleStorageContract.methods.getData().call();
    const number = await simpleStorageContract.methods.getNumber().call();
    setStoredData(data);
    setContractNumber(number);
  } catch (err) {
    setError('Failed to fetch data.');
  } finally {
    setIsLoadingContractData(false);
  }
}, [simpleStorageContract]);
Guidance
Expose a fetch function so consumers can refresh on user action or on network/account change. Keep loading and error state to guide UI decisions.
Testing idea
Mock web3 and the contract instance to assert that fetchContractData updates state correctly and handles rejection paths.
Key Takeaway

A hook centralizes contract logic, making components simpler and network behavior testable and consistent.

screens.title: Fetching data: fetchContractData explained
screens.subtitle: A walkthrough of the async fetch, error handling, and state updates

narration.text: Let's walk through fetchContractData, the function that reads values from the SimpleStorage contract. The function begins by checking that the contract instance exists. It sets a loading flag to true so the UI can show progress. Inside a try block it awaits simpleStorageContract. methods. getData(). call() to retrieve the stored string, then awaits getNumber(). call() for the pure number. Each returned value is stored in state with setStoredData and setContractNumber. If anything goes wrong — a malformed ABI, unreachable provider, or a wrong address — the catch block sets an error message so the UI can show feedback. Finally a finally block sets the loading flag to false to ensure the UI clears the spinner even when errors occur. A concrete example: if getData() returns 'Hello', setStoredData('Hello') leads the App JSX to render Stored Data: Hello. A common mistake is to forget the loading flag or to update state after the component has unmounted; cancelation or existence checks avoid setting state on unmounted components. Reflect: how might you signal the user to retry a failed fetch? Fetching data: fetchContractData explained means use loading, try/catch error handling, and final cleanup to make fetches predictable and user-friendly.. In practical terms, a walkthrough of the async fetch, error handling, and state updates. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Fetch lifecycle
keyIdea.text: Use loading, try/catch error handling, and final cleanup to make fetches predictable and user-friendly.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.4 › fetchContractData Walkthrough
fetchContractData structure
Guard existence → set loading → try to call methods → update state → handle error → finalize loading.
const fetchContractData = async () => {
  if (!simpleStorageContract) return;
  setIsLoadingContractData(true);
  try {
    const data = await simpleStorageContract.methods.getData().call();
    setStoredData(data);
    const number = await simpleStorageContract.methods.getNumber().call();
    setContractNumber(number);
  } catch (err) {
    setError('Failed to fetch data from SimpleStorage contract.');
  } finally {
    setIsLoadingContractData(false);
  }
};
Success path
Update state quickly and clear loading to reflect fresh on-chain data.
Failure path
Surface an error message and keep the UI stable; allow a retry action.
UI mapping
Use isLoading to show a spinner and error to show a friendly message; display storedData and contractNumber when available.
Example UI

Stored Data: {storedData || 'N/A'} — Contract Number: {contractNumber}

screens.title: Displaying retrieved state in React
screens.subtitle: Render values, format addresses and numbers, and show loading/error states

narration.text: Once your hook provides contract values, rendering them in React is straightforward but there are important UX considerations. Always show loading states while awaiting. call() results so users know data is being fetched. If an error occurs, show a friendly message and a retry affordance. When displaying raw blockchain data like addresses or large numbers, format them for readability: truncate addresses to a short left-right pattern and format big integers to human units where appropriate. For the SimpleStorage example, render Stored Data directly as a string and Contract Number as a normal integer. A common misconception is trusting raw blockchain output without formatting; long hex strings and big-number representations frustrate users. Also avoid rendering values until they are available; guard with conditional rendering to prevent undefined errors. For arrays or tuples returned by view functions, map over items and present them clearly. Example: Stored Data: Hello, Contract Number: 123. How will you present a loading state that is both clear and unobtrusive? Displaying retrieved state in React means show loading and errors, format addresses and large numbers, and avoid rendering undefined values to keep ui stable.. In practical terms, render values, format addresses and numbers, and show loading/error states. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Render rules
keyIdea.text: Show loading and errors, format addresses and large numbers, and avoid rendering undefined values to keep UI stable.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.4 › Display State
UI mapping examples
Use conditional rendering and loading flags to decide what to show. Keep text concise and human-friendly.
Loading state
isLoadingContractData ? 'Loading contract data...' : show values
Formatted values
Stored Data: {storedData || 'N/A'}
Contract Number: {contractNumber}
Address & Number handling
Truncate long addresses and format big integers to decimals or readable units when appropriate.
Truncate helper
Example: 0x1234...9abc — keep first 6 and last 4 characters for clarity.
Key Takeaway

Always translate raw blockchain values into concise, readable UI elements with loading and error feedback.

screens.title: Error handling and common mistakes
screens.subtitle: How to spot and fix the usual failures when reading contract data

narration.text: Reading contract data has predictable failure modes. The first is calling methods before the contract instance is initialized; this results in TypeError where methods is undefined. The fix is a simple existence guard: if (web3 && contractInstance) then call. The second is mismatched ABI and address — methods may be undefined or calls may decode incorrectly. Confirm the ABI came from the same compiled contract as the deployed address. The third category is network and provider errors: the node may be unreachable or the user may be on the wrong chain; handle these cases by surfacing a clear error and suggesting the expected network. Finally, forgetting to await. call() or omitting try/catch leads to unhandled promise rejections and broken UI. As an example, a missing address in the env file will prevent instantiation; log a descriptive message like 'Web3 not initialized or contract address missing.' A useful test: simulate each failure and verify your UI shows a helpful message and a retry option. What logging strategy will you use during development to surface ABI/address mismatches quickly? Error handling and common mistakes means guard against uninitialized web3, mismatched abi/address, provider/network errors, and unhandled promises. provide clear ui messages.. In practical terms, how to spot and fix the usual failures when reading contract data. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Failure modes
keyIdea.text: Guard against uninitialized web3, mismatched ABI/address, provider/network errors, and unhandled promises. Provide clear UI messages.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.4 › Errors & Fixes
TypeError: methods is undefined
Cause: contract instance not created. Fix: guard with if (web3 && address) and initialize instance in effect.
Mismatched ABI or Address
Cause: ABI doesn't match deployed bytecode or address points to another contract. Fix: confirm compilation output and deployment address.
Provider/Network Errors
Cause: node unreachable or wrong chain. Fix: surface clear UI guidance and suggest network switch or reconnect.
Debugging checklist
  • Check console logs for ABI/address mismatches.
  • Confirm import.meta.env provides the expected address at runtime.
  • Simulate network failure and ensure error state is shown to the user.
  • Wrap .call() in try/catch and set descriptive error messages.

screens.title: Performance and re-fetching strategies
screens.subtitle: When to re-run reads and how to avoid excessive calls

narration.text: Too many repeated reads can waste node resources and make the UI feel busy. Decide when to re-run reads by selecting an appropriate dependency list for useEffect: include web3, contractInstance, currentAccount, or chainId when those changes should trigger a fresh fetch. For user-driven updates, expose a refetch function so the user can refresh on demand. Memoize fetch functions with useCallback to avoid creating new references that retrigger effects. Debounce or throttle frequent triggers if your UI polls for updates at intervals. If you need near real-time updates, prefer event subscriptions when supported, or poll at a sensible interval with a clear loading indicator. A common misconception is that effects with no dependencies run only once; in practice, ensure your hook doesn't recreate functions on each render. Always balance freshness with cost and user expectations. Example strategy: fetch on mount, on network/account change, and when the user explicitly requests a refresh. How often will you poll in your dApp, if at all? Performance and re-fetching strategies means choose dependencies, expose a refetch function, and use memoization or throttling to control read frequency and cost.. In practical terms, when to re-run reads and how to avoid excessive calls. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Re-fetch guidance
keyIdea.text: Choose dependencies, expose a refetch function, and use memoization or throttling to control read frequency and cost.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.4 › Re-fetch Strategies
When to fetch
On mount, when web3/provider or contract instance changes, when account or chainId changes, or on explicit user request.
Memoize
Wrap fetch functions in useCallback so they only change when needed.
Expose refetch
Return a fetch function from your hook so the UI triggers refresh on actions like retry buttons.
Throttle & Poll
If polling, choose a sensible interval and show a loading indicator; avoid sub-second polling unless necessary.
Key Takeaway

Balance freshness with cost: prefer event subscriptions or on-demand refetches over constant polling when possible.

screens.subtitle: Step-by-step lab to implement the hook and show contract data in App.jsx

narration.text: This lab walks you through the steps described in the chapter to verify your understanding. First, confirm the SimpleStorage contract is deployed and you have its address. Save the ABI JSON to src/contracts/SimpleStorage. json and set VITE_SIMPLE_STORAGE_CONTRACT_ADDRESS in your. env. Next, implement the useSimpleStorage hook: import the ABI, read the address, create the contract instance in an effect, and implement fetchContractData to call getData and getNumber. Manage isLoadingContractData and error state so the UI informs users. Then import the hook into App. jsx, call it, and render Stored Data and Contract Number with clear loading and error messages. Test the common error: remove the address or stop your provider and observe the error handling. Finally, add a refresh control (UI-driven refetch) and test it. narration.text: Let's summarize the most important ideas. First, the ABI is the contract's interface description; web3 needs it to encode calls and decode results. Second, a contract's deployed address locates it on a specific network; both ABI and address must match the deployed bytecode. Third, web3. eth. Contract creates a local contract instance that exposes methods you call from JavaScript. Fourth, view and pure functions are read-only and free to call; use. call() to execute them and obtain returned values. Fifth, useEffect is the standard React mechanism to fetch contract data when web3, the contract instance, or the account changes. Finally, always guard calls, handle loading and errors, and format raw blockchain outputs for user-friendly display. Keep these fundamentals in mind as you build dApp UI that reads on-chain state reliably.

keyIdea.text: ABI + address → contract instance; .call() for reads; useEffect to fetch and update UI; guard and format values.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.4 › Key Concepts
ABI (Interface)
JSON that describes functions and events, required for encoding and decoding calls.
Contract Address
The deployed contract's unique network location; store per-network in env variables.
web3.eth.Contract
A local object created with ABI and address that exposes contract methods to call from JS.
view & pure
Read-only functions that do not consume gas and can be executed with .call().
.call()
Execute view/pure functions locally via a node and return a Promise with the result.
useEffect
React hook to fetch contract data on mount and when web3 or contract dependencies change.
Summary
Combine ABI, address, and web3.eth.Contract with .call() inside useEffect to read and render contract state reliably.
